body:
@khushvind This is amazing work, thank you! We definitely need something like this, and it's a smart algo.

I'm sorry I didn't get to look into it very well yet, but I did give it a try, and it seems there are a few issues. If you want, for replicating, I can give you the event stream I used, or, my scenario was something like: use a model with a relatively large context window (I used get-4o with 128k), make sure sessions are enabled[1], do stuff, then when the history gets to some 11k, stop it, config 4k in `max_input_tokens`, then restart. (or just change `max_input_tokens` to 4k in the debugger)

This will provoke it not only to apply summarize, but also do it consecutively before getting to a regular prompt, and it seems to behave unexpectedly in part, it loses information. Also, it doesn't seem to save the summary (my run ended with an error, but I'm not sure I see in the code where it saves them, even if it ends well?)

I can play with it more tomorrow I hope. Thank you for this!

[1] If you use opendevin via the UI, save `JWT_TOKEN=something` in env, it should do; just in case, enable `file_store="local"` with some `file_store_path` too in config.toml. If you use it with cli, `enable_cli_sessions=true`. I find that enabling/restoring sessions is a huge time saver for this kind of stuff, for... reasons. 😅
author: enyst

body:
Some thoughts, since we're at it: I think there are two major areas which have affected negatively performance in previous work.
- the prompt. It didn't always result in detailed enough information to guide the LLM for the next steps. This PR is using mostly the old prompt from PR 2021, and I'm hoping we can figure out something better. At least, I think we need it to give clear info to the LLM about what files it shouldn't check anymore, and what files it should continue working on. I don't remember if this exact version was doing any of those reliably, but anyway, I wonder if we could adapt something more of memGPT here? I'd favor completely ripping it up and replace, if we can.
- missing Recall action. This PR, like 2021, never retrieves the original events, thus must repeat them if it needs them. Now, this behavior in PR 2021 happened because that PR had gotten too large, I had to stop somewhere, and left recall/longterm memory for follow-up PRs. It might not have been the best idea ever, because this feature is *incomplete* without it. Also memGPT obviously relies on retrievals all the time (99% of all its memory work is recalling originals). That's totally as it should be, and we do plan to do that, but the question is: is it possible to be good enough without it? Cc: @xingyaoww 

FWIW in the swe-bench evals on PR 2021, I saw some tasks where the LLM was just restarting, as if it knew nothing. It wasn't using the summary! I think this was due to both prompt and recall. Since this PR is condensing 75% of the messages, leaving a few at the end, I think we won't see that anymore. Nevertheless, TBH if we still don't include recall, we do need to fix the prompt very well...

I found some decent tasks on swe-bench for this, I'm going to retrieve them and run them on this PR. I think I'll also add some recall and see how it goes then.
author: enyst

body:
@khushvind Thanks for your amazing work -- Let me know if this is ready for review again! 

I have a couple of ideas regarding how we can develop this:

1. We should develop a benchmark / a way to evaluate a "memory condensation algo quantitatively."
   - it could be something like a repurposed version of [Needle in a haystack](https://github.com/gkamradt/LLMTest_NeedleInAHaystack) For example, the input is a very long context prompt (128k tokens) with an instruction of "summarize everything, with a goal of XXX (that is related to the needle)"
   - re-use benchmarks from MemGPT https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.08560 to make sure we are getting comparable QA performance (using our condensation algo)
   - Running SWE-Bench with condensation enabled (sort of an ultimate metrics); I think getting the first two for eval is probably easier

2. I think this PR is probably ready to merge (but not enabled by default) after we can get comparable performance to MemGPT using benchmarks in their paper
3. Once we achieve comparable and better performance with condensation on the SWE-Bench, I think we can enable it by default.

body:
@tobitege this itself should be ready for review if it is ok with you! 

I'm experimenting with a slightly more general/cleaner way of building OpenDevin runtime images (e.g., using Jinja templates), which hopefully can provide a cleaner way to deal with these docker files in Python, and make it easier to extend these dockerfiles to different languages (e.g., nodejs).

> The way the above "nodejs" method is coded is that it doesn't require all the mamba stuff

The only previous reason for including `mamba` is that it can manage multiple versions of Python easily and can work out of the box when the base image does not contain the right Python version (e.g., py3.11), which is not your case for `ubuntu+py3.11`, though.

I guess if we get the Jinja template working nicely and cleanly, we could just start building every image with `ubuntu+py3.11` and get rid of Mamba completely to save space, and using the `mamba` workflow as a backup plan for "customized sandbox images."

Hey @neubig, thanks for asking, I read @li-boxuan's comment before and the example he gave. 

> Say you have L1,2,3,4, and you replace L3 with 2 new lines, and then you have L1,2,3,4,5, with L3 & L4 being new. We should only retain linting errors for L3-5 (inclusive).

One thing I am not very sure is that if we replace L3 with 2 new lines, will it cause new issues in other places inside of only these two lines? For example, if we delete a function defination, I think there will probably be some issues in other places if we use this function elsewhere. 

I still suggest to check the `lint_error` before and after the new modification and probably use my commit https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/3124/commits/02dab77e5f2e039f128452acb5cf28d6cc4ca30d ? Thanks!
author: bin123apple

body:
> > Say you have L1,2,3,4, and you replace L3 with 2 new lines, and then you have L1,2,3,4,5, with L3 & L4 being new. We should only retain linting errors for L3-5 (inclusive).
> 
> One thing I am not very sure is that if we replace L3 with 2 new lines, will it cause new issues in other places inside of only these two lines? For example, if we delete a function defination, I think there will probably be some issues in other places if we use this function elsewhere.
> 

That's a good point, so we DO need to run linter twice. I still think my [original comment](https://github.com/OpenDevin/OpenDevin/pull/3124#discussion_r1693877848) holds, though. I am worried about current approach causing regressions. Comparing errors using error message doesn't convince me. Taking `
F821 | undefined name [name]` for example. Let's say the original script is:

```python
def unused_bogus_func():
     undefined_func()

def func_to_modify():
     print('this function works')
```

Linter would report `test.py:2:5 F821 undefined name undefined_func`

and let's assume OpenDevin modifies it into:

```python
def unused_bogus_func():
     undefined_func()

def func_to_modify():
     undefined_func()
```

Linter would report `test.py:2:5 F821 undefined name undefined_func` and `test.py:5:5 F821 undefined name undefined_func`

In this example, the existing unused code contains a wrong function call, and LLMs might tend to learn from it and use the same wrong function call. Using the current approach in this PR (comparing error messages), this wrong edit by OpenDevin would be overlooked. Btw, this hypothetical example very likely wouldn't happen in swe-bench because swe-bench only targets high quality codebase. 

Similarly, there are some flake8 validation that only include a generic error message. They could be overlooked too (when both existing code and OpenDevin edits hit the same error).

That being said, one could argue that if an existing file has already made a specific linting issue, it's okay to make more of the same type. This doesn't sound correct but it might actually work well in swe-bench, a benchmark that we know existing code functions and thus any linting error before edits is false-positive.

To conclude, I wouldn't approve this PR due to the aforementioned issue, but I also hold no objection. It looks like it might improve the score on swe-bench a bit, although I suspect its general usability.
author: li-boxuan

body:
Thanks for pointing out the potential bug. 
> Linter would report `test.py:2:5 F821 undefined name undefined_func` and `test.py:5:5 F821 undefined name undefined_func`

Yes, this case will indeed be ignored by the current commit. 

It seems difficult to find a perfect solution. I’ve come up with two methods, but both have some potential edge cases.

***1. Also compare the line number before & after the lint.***

However, if some new lines are added. The `test.py:2:5` will change to `test.py:3:5`, which is not the same as the original lint_error.

***2. Also compare the number of the different types of errors.***

However, if the original error is fixed, and new error is imported. The new error will be ignored.

I haven't thought of a better solution for now either.

author: enyst

body:
> Please tell if I don't understand this correctly, AppConfig is already composed of those things, we have moved vars that used to be defined in the app_config into these smaller ones, and continued to split some more in time. Do you mean we should add more "buckets of settings" like them, such as a TaskConfig for iterations and the like? This is IMHO better, as best we can where they make sense, and it's the direction the code has been heading to. It would make things more readable, at least.

Correct me if @neubig think differently: Yes, if it make sense, I think at some point we can make `AppConfig` solely consists of a few config like `LLMConfig`, `AgentConfig` (or even making `LLMConfig` a part of `AgentConfig`), `RuntimeConfig` (the current `SandboxConfig`). So that it is possible for us to use them separately:

```python
config = AppConfig(
    task_config=task_config,
    agent_config=agent_config,
    runtime_config=agent_config
)

runtime = Runtime.from_config(runtime_config)
agent = Agent.from_config(agent_config)

state = run_controller(
    task=instruction,
    task_config=task_config,
    agent=agent,
    runtime=runtime
)
# OR use them altogether
state = run_controller(
    task=instruction,
    config=app_config
)

```

While `config=app_config` is sufficient for our OpenDevin web server, breaking this config into smaller components probably allows our components to be more reusable.

For example, people can just create a `Runtime` from `RuntimeConfig` separately (and only use it for their research purpose), without the need to create and understand how `AppConfig` works (we currently have one parameter in `AppConfig` that stay in the way of this..).

body:
~@tofarr is correct that this PR is a little special: you can't just pull this PR and `make run` - there might exist some existing `od_runtime:ubuntu_tag_22.04` image locally, and by default, OpenDevin will try to build from them first (but pip was NOT installed on those images). So you probably need:~

```
# Delete all OD images locally first
docker image ls --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}' | grep od_runtime | xargs docker rmi -f

# Create a build file
poetry run python3 opendevin/runtime/utils/runtime_build.py --base_image ubuntu:22.04 --build_folder containers/runtime --force_rebuild

# Build a "latest" Ubuntu image so that it will use this image locally
DOCKER_IMAGE_TAG=pip-fix bash ./containers/build.sh runtime OpenDevin arm64
```
---

These might be a little bit too complex (you'd need to install pip by yourselves based on ubuntu, which is not a perfect solution).

I'm thinking if it will be good that we switch the default image to "python:3.11-bookworm" with `python` and `pip` already pre-installed. I think the general idea we should go after is probably not to make our `Dockerfile.j2` as comprehensive as possible, rather, the user should change to a Docker image with all their wanted dependency installed.

A few more from Anthropic docs:

> The cache has a 5-minute lifetime, refreshed each time the cached content is used.

> Prompt Caching caches the full prefix
Prompt Caching references the entire prompt - tools, system, and messages up to and including the block designated with cache_control.

So we don't need to merge messages ourselves, instead set a checkpoint on the end message. Which is the end message is less clear to me. 😅 I have to test some more moving the messages checkpoint. 1024 tokens for Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3 Opus

body:
I noticed you replaced logger arguments with string interpolation. While IMHO string interpolation is easier to read, logger arguments can give other advantages, such as not having to interpolate strings at all depending on the log level and underlying implementation.

Is this a pattern we intend to use moving forward?
author: tofarr

body:
> I noticed you replaced logger arguments with string interpolation. While IMHO string interpolation is easier to read, logger arguments can give other advantages, such as not having to interpolate strings at all depending on the log level and underlying implementation.
> 
> Is this a pattern we intend to use moving forward?

Hey, indeed, I think there is some performance cost, in theory. The funny history here that when we initially implemented the logging system, it had only old-style %s formatting precisely for the reason you identified: to avoid computing the string when it won't be logged anyway due to the log level.

However, after that, in time, the codebase got f-strings all the time. Nobody liked the old-style! 😅 

Really, as you can see here I found only a few occurrences. Apparently these were the only ones left. 🤷 I frankly thought I'll find more, but no, they're f-strings already. (and I've definitely sinned too!)

Yes, IMHO it's time to admit we can't swim against this tide, too many people do it this way for too many years.. So my suggestion is to go the other way around: use nice syntax; then if and when we will see performance issues tracked to it, we can reconsider using lazy evaluation on a case by case basis - if we find something bad enough.

Actually the thing that this PR does remove is the ability to input a custom model given a provider (e.g., `openrouter/some-random-model-maybe-not-in-docs`). Do you think this is OK? I can't see the reasons why the user would want to do such a thing in the first place

@amanape There is this tricky thing where liteLLM interprets the model names like "openai/something" as a hint to route the `completion` call to an openai-compatible endpoint, which they build according to base_url or provider-specific url, and ending with /v1, in other words they build some API URL which they know accepts messages in OpenAI format, _because_ the user added "openai" prefix. (In that case it also makes sure that the parameters are in the right format, I think)

I don't know if that has relevance for openrouter. I know our users needed it in some cases, like CommandR and/or Cohere where the prefix worked, its missing did not.

My point is that typing in the box was necessary to add /openai to some prefixes. Maybe it's fine if it's still possible via custom model, though.

Sorry for typing in a closed issue, just a quick thought and I'll take it these days elsewhere for further thinking/testing.

My hope for this particular stuck check was that we can get rid of it, replace the hard-coded error with figuring out there was a syntax error from the runtime, or the ast, or jupyter. That said, when you're happy with it, feel free to take it in and let's try it.

I've picked up your suggestion to also check IPythonRunCellAction's during stuck checks in the `_eq_no_pid` with regard to its `code` attribute.

author: tobitege

body:
As discussed in private, I now think that you are absolutely correct that we should not need `thought` for an edit action. An edit has a lot of information that is or should be clear, and we can compare it even if the LLM doesn't "think" anything alongside the edit command.

And if the thoughts were very different, the only reason that could matter is if these thoughts, sent again in the context next time, can "convince" the LLM to change its approach away from the edit that gives the error. If we could guess from the 'thoughts' that the LLM has good chances to change, it may make sense to keep it in the comparison. But we can't really: after all, the LLM _sent the same edit_ regardless. We can just give it one more chance (above 3), and we already do 4, I think. 🤔

@ryanhoangt @ketan1741 
I'm debugging this a bit, and I don't know yet enough answers we need, but just so you know:
- The PR is merged. Please see here for delegates trajectories on a simple test: [HuggingFace](https://huggingface.co/spaces/engelnyst/OpenHands-evaluation?filepaths=outputs%2Fswe_bench_lite%2FCoActPlannerAgent%2Fclaude-3-5-sonnet%4020240620_maxiter_30_N_v1.0-no-hint%2Foutput.jsonl&row_idx=0) or attached [CoActPlannerAgent.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/17019905/CoActPlannerAgent.zip)

- IMHO `django__django-10914` looks like a fluke. It's funny... the agent has to find FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS, in the task FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSION is used interchangeably with FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS, and the agent read the right file, but 1) on `main` it concluded that it has FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS and modifies it, 2) on branch it concluded it cannot find FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSION so it has to add it and fails the task.
In the example test above it succeeded (repeatedly) on the PR branch. 🤷 

- In part, we are making CodeAct a delegate and it's not yet ready for it. 😅 For example, a thing that happens is that it's using `get_user_message()` [here](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/blob/2a10ff13741dc47452240787b06def2463d38903/agenthub/codeact_agent/codeact_agent.py#L190) which has to return a MessageAction. But a delegate doesn't have any MessageAction, and the method has no protection for delegates (it doesn't stop at `start_id` or AgentDelegateAction) so it's hijacking a MessageAction from the parent agent. This shouldn't happen (fix coming up).
It doesn't influence anything else, but there might be other issues of this kind...?
FWIW other delegates use something [like this](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/blob/d886bf7e2bddb938ef4745b92f6ca58028ee07b0/agenthub/browsing_agent/browsing_agent.py#L207).

body:
@ColeMurray We wrote in the same time 😄.

You're right, that's it. OK, that is not within the scope of this PR.

Back to the PR: the other issue here is that we merge TextContents into a single string per message, and that doesn't work well with prompt caching. Allow me to expand why. We have 4 checkpoints usually, the max allowed by Anthropic. The first is the system message, the second is initial user message, these work well and are permanently in place.

```
CodeActAgent LEVEL 0 LOCAL STEP 2 GLOBAL STEP 2
21:57:01 - openhands:INFO: llm.py:515 - Cost: 0.00 USD | Accumulated Cost: 0.03 USD
Input tokens: 4
Output tokens: 95
Input tokens (cache write): 268
Input tokens (cache read): 4610

```

Then third and fourth messages marked for caching are the last message in history, and the one before it. But the last message in history always has a [REMINDER added](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/blob/c5e89be6dec3a6d1eb1bdc80a52046004457337c/agenthub/codeact_agent/codeact_agent.py#L288).
That means the last message with reminder is cached in one step, and it's _changed_ in the next step (because it doesn't include reminder anymore). This is a permanent cache miss:
```

CodeActAgent LEVEL 0 LOCAL STEP 3 GLOBAL STEP 3

21:57:48 - openhands:INFO: llm.py:515 - Cost: 0.00 USD | Accumulated Cost: 0.04 USD
Input tokens: 4
Output tokens: 53
Input tokens (cache write): 380
Input tokens (cache read): 4610
...
CodeActAgent LEVEL 0 LOCAL STEP 7 GLOBAL STEP 7

21:59:04 - openhands:INFO: llm.py:515 - Cost: 0.01 USD | Accumulated Cost: 0.06 USD
Input tokens: 4
Output tokens: 124
Input tokens (cache write): 1798
Input tokens (cache read): 4610
```

This run will never cache more than 4610 tokens 😅. According to the links you posted, the messages must not change from one step to the other (of course):
> Changes that can break the cache include modifying any content

But the last message does always change, adding once the reminder and removing it next time. This works fine with Pydantic's serialization (if vision was enabled thing), because it doesn't merge the text content: it has 2 dicts for 2 TextContent objects, first is cached, the second is the reminder that will change. So that's fine, the first will be found in cache.

We can fix this in multiple ways, I suppose: instead of caching the last and previous-to-last message, we could cache the previous-to-last and the one before it; or, we could try to not merge the strings for text, serialize them as different dicts, like `model_dump` is doing; or, we could hack the exclusion of the reminder text ... I don't favor the last, otherwise dunno, what do you think?

body:
I'm not sure if we should let the agents access the event stream via State, or directly. The current draft does it directly, it has agents store a reference to the stream, and the effect seems like... a lot of passing around. It would be straightforward to give a ref to the `state` and be done, everyone would go from `state.history` -> `state.event_stream`.
On the other hand, the event stream is a "permanent" fixture of the environment where agents run, our "source of truth", it's a little odd to store it in the runtime state (even if we wouldn't pickle it). What do you think? @rbren @neubig
author: enyst

body:
Giving the event_stream directly to the agent makes me a little nervous. There are lots of things it could hypothetically do (like publish events and subscribe to events) that really should be handled by the agent_controller.

The agent should only really need a static list of historical events. I wonder if there's a way to do that without duplicating state
author: rbren

body:
@rbren Maybe strictly subscribing isn't quite possible, but what is the purpose of the subscription mechanism, if only a few well behaved components respect it, and more than a dozen others access the source freely outside the mechanism?

> The agent should only really need a static list of historical events. I wonder if there's a way to do that without duplicating state

- We could get a minimally processed list of events, as an actual `list` with events, [like this](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/blob/dd228c07e05b6908bc1d15dde8f8025284a9ef47/openhands/memory/history.py#L150). What if we never save it, but re-compute it every step, does that make it better? 😅 
Minimally processed might mean: basic filtering yes, not sure about delegates filters, summaries no, retrieval no. Then we need an intermediary, like History or the new PromptManager class, only we may want it to work `from that list` + State, to the elements that the agent needs in the prompt.

- What if we don't send the agent a list of Events, but a list of Messages? Probably I'm missing something, but we have a Message class, as a helper serializing events for insertion in the prompt. As of now, it's not possible to go the other way around, but it could be: if we could convert it back to the Event... maybe we can send the agent a list of Messages. Hey, that's not a copy! 😅 Agent helpers, like PromptManager, might need to convert back and do what they may still need to do.

- Are you sure it's a _static_ list of events? It's almost fully static today. But an agent with memory will not have a static history. 🤔
author: enyst

body:
Some good questions here!

> what is the purpose of the subscription mechanism, if only a few well behaved components respect it

I actually think it should be very open to anyone publishing/subscribing--but specifically agents should be excluded there, at least with the current centralized AgentController. But you have me thinking that maybe that's a mistake. Going to think more on this.

> What if we don't send the agent a list of Events, but a list of Messages?

The event -> message conversion could definitely be a helpful utility, but we lose a lot of information there, so I do think we need to send the raw events


> Are you sure it's a static list of events? It's almost fully static today. But an agent with memory will not have a static history.

IMO we should pass the complete static history to the agent in Python, and then let the agent decide when and where to condense before it passes it to the LLM. Probably we implement a reusable Memory that several agents use, but I'd like for different agents to be able to experiment with their own mem mgmt

body:
To clarify a bit the issue here, for the record: since the introduction of vision support, we have changed the format we send messages to the LLM. The format we started sending was the openai-compatible format for vision, like:
```
{'content': [{'type': 'text', 'text': 'Ask me what your task is'}, ...], 'role': 'user'}
```
It has a list of dicts of content types, instead of the old simpler format, where 'content' is just a single string. Content types are 'text' and 'image_url'.

Things seemed to work, until they didn't: in reality, as @tobitege found and fixed already, multiple providers don't support this format or not fully. They appear to support this for `role: user`, but not for `role: system`, and sadly, not for `role: assistant`. The fix did what was necessary: since this situation requires us to support 2 kinds of serialization, basically, in some way, pending future fixes from litellm/providers. Tobi did the hard work on this and restored the non-vision format so that things work.

This PR merely aims to simplify the first take on this:
- it settles on a compromise: serialize `user` messages in vision-like format, but the rest not, if vision isn't enabled. This works in all cases I've seen so far.
- it refactors how we do serialization: it was in two places, now it's in one place, pydantic decorated Message serializers.

Note: I think we had some code in serialization that was used only in integration tests. This PR moves it to tests. IMHO the code has become way too complex, and we'll be happier if we keep the core code do core stuff, and the tests do tests stuff.

I think that a base method should have reasonable defaults, and it seems to me that a 10 minute timeout on http connections is not a reasonable default. In any case, having the timeout based on a time rather than a number of iterations seems more intuitive and easier to understand.

If there are cases where we need a 10 minute timeout on a http connection, I think this should be where we apply the custom parameters for that case, rather than making that the default.

body:
> I think that a base method should have reasonable defaults, and it seems to me that a 10 minute timeout on http connections is not a reasonable default. In any case, having the timeout based on a time rather than a number of iterations seems more intuitive and easier to understand.
> 
> If there are cases where we need a 10 minute timeout on a http connection, I think this should be where we apply the custom parameters for that case, rather than making that the default.

The nice thing about the exponential variant is, that if it was a transient error, you may get past it within under 10 seconds, as example.
When you put in a fixed value, then it will always wait that amount of time before retrying, like you create a minimum wait time of 2 minutes?
author: tobitege

body:
Also - using number of iterations means the overall time does not include the actual time of the http request - (which times out at 15 minutes if I'm not mistaken).

For example, suppose we connect to an endpoint that sends or received no data but leaves the connection open - then our timeout for each connection is 15 minutes by default. So in this case our system will exponentially ramp up the wait time to 1 minute between attempts while also taking 15 minutes for each attempt 15 times = ~240 minutes
author: tofarr

body: The exponential variant is still in place with the timeout - so you can still get passed it in less than 10 seconds - the way this change works is that rather than checking a number of iterations when determining whether to retry, it now checks the time

body:
- LLM: replaced `after` with `before_sleep` retry param
- use new `OperationCancelled` exception instead of `UserCancelledError`
- extended `test_llm.py` tests with exception handling tests
- changed logging of token counts to be on a single line, like cost

@enyst - Thanks for the valuable feedback, I'll try to address it here in one comment instead of spread out:
The long-time use of the `after` in the decorator was not quite optimal, as it is called for BOTH successes and fails.

The circumstance, that the keyboard interrupt (like logged in your PR) didn't "make it through" is, imo,
a side effect of the new shutdown handlers, not the LLM's `@retry` decorator.
E.g. `KeyboardInterrupt` wouldn't have been intercepted either way as it is not in the list of retried exceptions.

The remedy here was to use the `should_exit()` method and then to raise a (new) `OperationCancelled`
exception, that ends the retry loop (the initially used `UserCancelledError` was inappropriate, I think,
as it could be used in relation to agents/UI flow).

I've added multiple new tests to `test_llm.py` to test the exception handling, incl. keyboard interrupt.

The exception handling in CodeActAgent was required - and probably needs to be moved to agent_controller? - for
the fact that if an exception got through, it broke everything.

body:
Sharing some updates, I think we are close to having the editing PR merged! It seems the upper bound of the new editing is higher than our current main:

- **Performance-wise**: On editing PR iteration v2.4 - We got to 77/300 (25.67%) w/ sonnet by increasing the max iteration to 100 (default of our app i believe) with avg 41 turns. The main baseline got 63 / 300 (21.00%) using the same 100 iterations requiring avg 43 turns (there were some performance degradation on our main branch since `24 sep` eval - @neubig is currently helping me locating the issue now).
- **Cost-wise**:
    - A bump to 100 max turns increases costs to about 1$ per instance (about where we were when there was no prompt caching), whereas we previously measured sonnet costs about $0.3 per issue (but there was some bug in the metric calculation so this could be under-estimate)
    - We CAN use the default agent model as an editing model without incurring cost increases.
        - On editing PR iteration v2.4
            - Avg. agent cost per instance: 0.92 USD
            - Avg. editor cost per instance: 0.12 USD
            - Avg. total cost per instance: 1.04 USD
        - On main baseline (where no LLM-based editing is used):
            - Avg. num of turns per instance: 43.02
            - Avg. agent cost per instance: 1.27 USD
            - Avg. editor cost per instance: 0.00 USD
            - Avg. total cost per instance: 1.27 USD
- Increase the file-context window from 100 to 300 lines doesn't work
    - anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 WITH 300 lines file ctx: 63/300 = 21%
    - anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620: 77/300 = 25.7%
- New editing PR seems to suffer less from exceeding 200k context window of Claude
    - for editing v2.4: 1/300
    - for main branch baseline: 12/300

ALL the experiments above are performed using anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620, with one run each (can't afford to run it multiple times now we increase the turns to 100 - back at square 1 where each run costs 300 bucks).

I'll gradually move pieces from the editing PR into separate PR to make it easier for code review & fixing test cases

@neubig This PR is not ready for review, but its specification as of now, is. The way it's heading, this is how it could work:

- [config.template.toml](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/pull/4109/files#diff-8647bc42ec0a03f8f8c7079fc2cdefdd9f3a0bc2ef3f199b1fd6d5670ae27192R168)

in particular,
>  Then, in order to use a named LLM ([llm.your_name_for_gpt-4o], you can:
> 1. Without Router:
>     - specify the `'llm.<model_name>'` in the `--llm_config=...` or `-l=...` command line option, if running from CLI
>     - or, if you want, specify a `llm.<model_name>` in the default Agent configuration, e.g.:
>          `[agent]`
>          `llm_config='llm.<model_name>'`
>     - or, in the configuration of a specific Agent:
>        `[agent.BrowsingAgent]`
>        `llm_config='llm.<model_name>'`
> 2. With Router:
>     - specify the llm configurations to use as a list of 'llm.<model_name>', in the router section, e.g.:
>        `[router_config]`
>        `default_model='llm.<model_name>'`
>        `model_list = ['llm.<model_name>', ...]`
>  Any of the options above, if specified, will take precedence over the settings in the default 'llm' group.
> 
> ### IMPORTANT:
> If Router is used, it takes precedence over ALL the agent specific or default LLM config.
> ONLY the LLMs in the router config will be used.

Features:
- Fallbacks would work.
- Retries would be mostly predefined by litellm (customizable for `requests per minute` iirc), it handles that itself.
- We would need to implement `tokens per minute` limit, for LLMConfig.

Is this too confusing? They're two different ways of defining and of using configurations. The idea with this approach, if we want Router, it would represent a first step, then as we figure out how it should interact with the rest, we can add closer integration.

The alternative: 😅 
Or we could rip the bandaid, and try to build on Router alone. Then I don't have answers yet, how everything could work.

`event_to_dict` is used a lot, it's sent to the runtime, it's also sent to the UI, it contains more stuff from the event, than the LLM needs or knows.

`event_to_memory` is used only by planner agent and micro agent, to serialize events for their prompt, just before their prompt is sent to the LLM. It includes already less attributes than `event_to_dict`, to not confuse the LLM with our backend stuff. Here are the uses: only [six uses](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3AAll-Hands-AI%2FOpenHands%20event_to_memory&type=code), of which two are tests.

body:
@xingyaoww this is what Sonnet says about it, does that help?

-----

The problem lies in where you're trying to execute `chmod`. You're copying `resistant_script.sh` into the runtime's sandboxed environment (`runtime.config.workspace_mount_path_in_sandbox`) and then attempting to change its permissions *inside* the sandbox.  The sandbox likely has restricted permissions, preventing the `chmod` command from succeeding.

You should make the script executable *before* copying it into the sandbox.

```python:tests/runtime/test_bash.py
def test_process_resistant_to_multiple_sigint(temp_dir, box_class, run_as_openhands):
    # ... existing code ...

    with open(f'{temp_dir}/resistant_script.sh', 'w') as f:
        f.write(script_content)

    # Make the script executable *before* copying
    os.chmod(f'{temp_dir}/resistant_script.sh', 0o755)  # Or 0o775 depending on your needs

    runtime.copy_to(
        os.path.join(temp_dir, 'resistant_script.sh'),
        runtime.config.workspace_mount_path_in_sandbox,
    )

    # ... rest of the test ...

```
This change ensures that the script has the correct permissions before it's placed in the sandboxed environment, avoiding the permission error.  Using `os.chmod` directly is generally preferred over running `chmod` as a separate command.  The `0o755` permission gives execute permission to the owner, group, and others (read and execute for owner, read and execute for group and others).  Adjust this (e.g., to `0o700` or `0o775`) if you need different permissions.

  * load /app, redirect to /
* If there's an invalid session token

  * load /app, show an error message and redirect to /
* If there's a valid session token

  * load /app, show the ongoing session

body:
@li-boxuan I updated the description and the title (the title is hard 😅 ).

Basically, what you say: yes, let's split and put it this way. This PR proposes two things:
- fill in with it the `thought` attribute of the AgentDelegateAction, instead of leaving it empty. It will be used by the parent later. Currently it's just absent when the action is parsed.
- send to the delegate as `task` only the contents in _execute_browse_ tags. Instead of inserting in its "task", this "thought". The contents of the "thought" are the rest of the response that the LLM of the parent returned (outside the execute tag). The `task` will be inserted as "{goal}" in the delegate's prompt template. The `thought` will be inserted in the parent's history.

For the record, the history of the main agent is also unintended IMHO:
```

<execute_browse>
Understood. I will use the browsing tool to find the current Vice President of the USA.. I should start with: Search for "current Vice President of the USA" on Google

This is the entirety of the action in the parent's history: since the whole content was in `task`, the serialization in codeact puts it all in _execute browse_ tags, plus a newline for the empty `thought`.

I would expect:
```
Understood. I will use the browsing tool to find the current Vice President of the USA.. I should start with: 
<execute_browse>
Search for "current Vice President of the USA" on Google

author: xingyaoww

body:
> @enyst Is it possible to calculate cache write by doing `total_tokens - cached_tokens` so we don't need to handle this specifically for anthropic?

It's not _exactly_ that difference. 😅 Anthropic doesn't write to cache automatically, we need to tell it what to cache and what to leave alone. And we do: we always leave out _at least_ this little bit that would result in cache misses all the time if it was included: [funny variable bit of context](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/blob/a3c49538fca459c93cbb8c655bf4d360601c2029/openhands/agenthub/codeact_agent/codeact_agent.py#L277).

I honestly don't think it's worth bothering with the reminder at this point, since well, we are likely heading towards a lot more variance in the context so we'll have more cache-missing stuff to handle.
author: enyst

body:
In other words, unlike Deepseek, Anthropic has 3 costs for input tokens:
- cache writes (iirc +25% regular cost)
- cache reads  (10% of regular cost)
- regular input tokens (regular cost)

We need to use all 3 currently, because of our reminder has to be the regular category, not included in caches.

body:
Hey @danicruz0415, thanks for your input. To answer your questions:

> 1. do you think its best to keep all the translations in one file?

No, I do not. The recommended way in the official documentation would be to have a translations file per language. (e.g., `en.json` contains the English translations, `de.json` contains the German translations, etc). I definitely think we should look for ways to break down the translation files for the future.

> 2. If so, do you think its worth grouping the elements on the Json structure itself?

Yes, that is a good alternative and I can see it improve DX for the time being. As a side note, since the major UI changes, there are actually a lot of translations that are no longer required, but left over. In reality, there are only a few keys currently being used.

> 3. What would be the standard to leave the resources pending to be translated?

As is. IF we had individual translation files, it would be easy for other individuals to extend it.

> 4. How could I support without generating git conflicts?

I think one strategy would be to agree on certain routes/components to work on, on separate PRs. There will be some conflict since some routes re-use certain components, but it would expected and shouldn't be too difficult to resolve. You can see a basic map of the FE here:

https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/tree/main/frontend#project-structure

Thanks a lot for taking this up! Feel free to open another PR mentioning the routes/components you plan to cover

body:
The LLM section itself is for a specific model. These fallback scenarios may save typing, but end up potentially mixing values from different sections that imo shouldn't.
Non-present values in a custom llm section should only fall back to data class defaults, otherwise it is more complex, not easier, to find out where a value comes from.
E.g. a `max_output_tokens` value might be left out in "[llm.sonnet]" but suddenly get a value from the "[llm]" section which is just wrong as it is for a different model.
Then it should fallback to the default dataclass value.
Not to mention, that changing the model in the UI completely makes the toml file an unknown in which values are taken.
author: tobitege

body:
@tobitege You make good points, and I think there is a solution for the first: the case happens because you need `max_out_tokens` for the LLM in `[llm]`, then you can name that LLM, right? e.g. `[llm.llama]`. Then they override as you wish, if I understand correctly: the attributes of llama with llama, claude with claude.

A model is optional in the `[llm]` section. We can use it or not, at all. As you say, if it helps to actually choose exactly what you want to choose: then name that group.

The issue with how the UI works with toml is [tracked here](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands/issues/3220). Just to note here:

Custom LLM configs were developed for CLI, not UI. I'm pretty sure they did not interfere with the UI at all until - as you pointed out recently in slack - the unexpected happened: setting one as "agent" LLM made it actively used with the UI too. That was, as far as I know, an unintended use case, and frankly I didn't even think it could happen until you mentioned it. I didn't even get to test it yet. This issue is not about that.

I think sorting it all out will not be trivial, but if I were to guess, probably the solutions for the interplay between UI and toml will be based on:
- have LLM settings (all of them or almost) in the UI. That should solve some issues, and, importantly,
- the suggestion in the linked topic, to actually save in the toml file when you override from the UI; and of course read it, not parts, not unintently, but read it all, should fix many of these things.

IMHO, the way it works now is mostly workable, except for that case - agent llm. I'm not sure how we should address that, without very significant changes.
